title: 17 hours awake = drunk

strategy.viewer: Curious adults who have pulled an all-nighter and wonder how bad it really gets; clicks for the extreme record and the 'drunk brain' hook.
strategy.hook: Seventeen hours awake is like being drunk; eleven days and your brain starts sleeping while you are awake: a familiar fact against an impossible one.
strategy.promise: What really happens in your brain from hour 0 to hour 264 without sleep, with the real cases (Tripp, Gardner) and the science.
strategy.payoff: A brain that will not sleep starts sleeping in pieces (local sleep, microsleeps) while awake, and without full sleep its cleaning flow (glymphatic) never completes.
strategy.takeaway: Stay awake long enough and your brain starts sleeping without you.

scenes.text: Seventeen hours without sleep makes you perform about like a driver at point zero five.
Study after study found the same thing: your reaction speed slides with every hour awake.
At twenty-four hours, it is about point one, over the legal limit in many countries.
And caffeine does not fix it. It only hides the signal.
The full story is on the channel. Subscribe for the next one.

titles: What 264 Hours Without Sleep Does to Your Brain
Your Brain After 11 Days Without Sleep
Why Your Brain Starts Sleeping While Awake

youtube.description:
What happens to your brain after 24, 48, 72 hours without sleep, and beyond? From the drunk-like brain to microsleeps, hallucinations, and the clean-up your brain does at night, with the real cases of Peter Tripp (1959) and Randy Gardner (1963).

In this video:
- Awake too long
- The drunk brain
- The brain that naps
- Seeing things
- The night shift

FAQ
How long can a person stay awake? The best-known documented experiment is 264 hours (Gardner, 1963-64); it is dangerous and not recommended.
What is a microsleep? A lapse of a fraction of a second up to about 30 s when the brain briefly sleeps.
Does sleep clean the brain? In mice, the space between cells widens ~60% in sleep and waste clears faster (Xie 2013).

Tell me in the comments: what is your longest time awake?

Sources: Dawson & Reid 1997, Nature 388; Williamson & Feyer 2000, Occup Environ Med; Vyazovskiy et al. 2011, Nature 472; Nir et al. 2017, Nature Medicine 23; Yoo et al. 2007, Current Biology (amygdala) and Nature Neuroscience (memory); Xie et al. 2013, Science 342; Shokri-Kojori et al. 2018, PNAS 115; Gulevich, Dement & Johnson 1966, Arch Gen Psychiatry (Gardner).
